brand.title: IQVIA (Production)
brand.subtitle: Knowledge Check — Introduction to Social Selling Techniques

questions.question: What are the two axes that form the foundation of the Social Style Selling framework?
choices: Introversion vs. Extroversion and Logic vs. Emotion
Task vs. People and Ask vs. Tell
Speed vs. Accuracy and Detail vs. Overview
Relationship vs. Transaction and Direct vs. Indirect
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly right—the two axes (Task/People on the Y axis and Ask/Tell on the X axis) create the mental grid for reading any buyer.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The framework is built on two specific questions: what drives their behavior (Task or People), and how do they get what they want (Ask or Tell)? These axes intersect to create the four styles.

questions.question: Which of the following is a signature question that an Analytical buyer is most likely to ask?
choices: What are the results and outcomes?
How does this work and how was it measured?
Who else is using this solution?
Why should I trust you over alternatives?
questions.feedback_correct: You've got it—Analyticals lead with 'How?' because they focus on process, accuracy, and data-driven decision-making.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Each style has a distinct signature question. Analyticals ask 'How?' (process and accuracy), while Drivers ask 'What?' (results), Expressives ask 'Who?' (people and vision), and Amiables ask 'Why?' (relationships and fit).

questions.question: What does a Driver typically do when they feel pressured or when the conversation goes off track?
choices: They ask for more time and detailed data to evaluate
They become argumentative and push back hard
They take control of the meeting
They go quiet and withdraw from the conversation
questions.feedback_correct: Correct—Drivers' pressure behavior is to take control of the meeting when they feel the conversation is not moving toward outcomes.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Each style shows a different pressure behavior: Drivers take control, Analyticals ask for more time and data, Expressives get argumentative, and Amiables go quiet and withdraw. Recognizing these signals helps you course-correct early.

questions.question: What is the primary reason the Social Style model is built on observed behavior rather than personality tests?
choices: Personality tests are too expensive and time-consuming
It allows you to watch how someone communicates in real time without psychoanalyzing them
Personality tests have been proven scientifically unreliable
Observable behavior is more entertaining to discuss in sales conversations
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—the model is grounded in what you can actually see and hear: how someone asks for things, what they pay attention to, how much emotion they show.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The foundation of this model is practical observation, not psychology or labels. You're watching behavior (how they communicate, what questions they ask, their emotional expression) and using that to guide your approach in real time.

questions.question: An Amiable buyer is showing signs of withdrawal and giving very short answers. What should you do?
choices: Push harder with data and evidence to convince them
Speed up the meeting and move toward a decision quickly
Slow down, acknowledge what is happening, and shift your approach to rebuild rapport
Ask them more detailed questions about the features and specifications
questions.feedback_correct: You're applying the framework perfectly—catching the early warning sign (withdrawal) lets you shift before rapport is damaged, not rebuild trust you didn't need to lose.
questions.feedback_incorrect: When you notice a pressure behavior or sudden drop in engagement (like an Amiable going quiet), that's your signal to pause and adjust. Early intervention prevents bigger problems down the road.

questions.question: You are speaking with a buyer who is animated, telling stories about their vision, and wants to know who else is using your solution. What is their most likely Social Style?
choices: Analytical
Driver
Expressive
Amiable
questions.feedback_correct: That's the read—high emotion, storytelling, vision-focused, and asking 'Who?' are all hallmarks of an Expressive buyer.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Expressives are animated, tell stories, focus on vision and possibilities, and ask 'Who?' because they think in terms of people and teams. Amiables are warm but soft-spoken; Drivers are direct and results-focused; Analyticals ask detailed questions about process.

questions.question: When selling to an Analytical buyer, what is the worst approach you could take?
choices: Offering clear options and specific next steps
Asking detailed, logical questions and providing evidence throughout
Getting personal, moving too fast, or presenting without rigorous justification
Taking time to explain how you got to this meeting
questions.feedback_correct: You understand the mismatch—Analyticals need rigor, evidence, and time to evaluate. Skipping those elements damages trust immediately.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Analyticals feel confident when you prepare detailed questions, use evidence, give them evaluation time, and justify your process logically. Personal connection and vague claims do the opposite.

questions.question: Your own Social Style can cause you to naturally shut down a buyer of a different style. What is the key first step to prevent this?
choices: Hire a sales coach to observe all your calls
Become aware of your own defaults and how they might land differently on other styles
Only meet with buyers who share your exact Social Style
Use a personality test to determine your type once and for all
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—awareness of your own style and its blind spots is where versatility begins, because you can't adjust what you don't see.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The course emphasizes that your natural selling approach lands differently on different buyers. Self-awareness of your defaults is the foundation for choosing when and how to adjust.

questions.question: What does versatility actually mean in the context of Social Style Selling?
choices: Changing your personality completely for each buyer type
Being agreeable and flexible about everything the buyer wants
Deliberately adjusting your communication approach to reduce friction and help the buyer feel understood
Using different sales techniques depending on how much money the deal is worth
questions.feedback_correct: Perfect—versatility is a deliberate, conscious shift in how you communicate, not a shift in who you are, and it builds trusted advisor status across all styles.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Versatility means removing friction by adjusting your communication so the buyer doesn't have to work as hard to connect with you. It's a discipline and a skill, not a personality change or vague niceness.

questions.question: A buyer you are meeting with shows low emotion, gives direction quickly, and seems most interested in speed and outcomes. You later discover they have an Expressive adjacent style. How will this adjacent style most likely modify their core behavior?
choices: They will ask more questions and slow down their decision-making
They will become more methodical and data-focused
They will be more direct and even faster-paced than a pure Driver
They will be warmer and more willing to engage in conversation than a pure Driver
questions.feedback_correct: That's exactly right—an Expressive adjacent softens the pure Driver's edge by adding warmth and conversational engagement while keeping the results focus intact.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Adjacent styles sit next to the primary style on the grid and soften or modify how the primary shows up. A Driver with Expressive adjacent stays results-focused but noticeably warmer; an Analytical with Amiable adjacent stays methodical but more relationship-conscious.
